summary: In this episode, the hosts discuss the 'five(ish) falls of angels,' exploring how various angelic rebellions are depicted in Scripture and corrected from pagan myths. They begin with the fall of the devil, who becomes the lord of death, and then examine the fall of angels who gave forbidden knowledge to humanity, leading to the Nephilim. The third fall involves the origin of unclean spirits from the dead Nephilim. The fourth fall is the Tower of Babel, where God assigns nations to angelic beings who later accept worship. The fifth fall is the casting down of Satan during Christ's ministry. Throughout, they emphasize that these rebellions are ongoing and that humanity is drawn into them, but God uses even demonic affliction for repentance.

entities.title: Devil
entities.summary: The fallen angel who rebelled against God and became the lord of death, tempting humanity.

entities.title: Satan
entities.summary: A title meaning 'adversary,' possibly a distinct figure from the devil, who accuses in the divine council and falls during Christ's ministry.

entities.title: Baal
entities.summary: A Canaanite god whose myth of succession is corrected in Scripture; often mentioned in the Old Testament.

entities.title: Enlil
entities.summary: A Babylonian god who was overthrown by Marduk; Isaiah uses his name (Helel) to refer to the devil.

entities.title: Og, King of Bashan
entities.summary: A giant king whose iron bed is described in Deuteronomy, linked to pagan ritual beds.

concepts.title: Succession Myth
concepts.summary: A common ancient Near Eastern story where a younger god overthrows the most high god, which Scripture corrects by showing the rebellion fails.

concepts.title: Devil as Lord of Death
concepts.summary: After the fall in Genesis 3, the devil is cursed to eat dust and becomes associated with death and the underworld.

concepts.title: Nephilim and Giants
concepts.summary: The offspring of fallen angels and human women, leading to giants and unclean spirits after their death.

concepts.title: Tower of Babel and the Nations
concepts.summary: God confuses languages and assigns nations to angelic beings (sons of God) as a punishment, but these beings later accept worship, becoming territorial spirits.

concepts.title: Fall of Satan in Christ's Ministry
concepts.summary: Christ's ministry causes Satan to be cast down from heaven, giving authority to believers over demons.

claims.text: The devil cannot overthrow God by force; his rebellion is internal, dethroning God in hearts and minds, and he attacks humanity out of envy.
The serpent in Genesis 3 is not a literal snake but the devil, a shining, deceiving angel, as shown by Hebrew wordplay.
The spirits of the dead Nephilim become the unclean demons that afflict people in the New Testament.
The Tower of Babel was not a failed attempt to reach heaven but a ziggurat built to bring gods down and manipulate them through idolatry.
Satan's fall from heaven occurs during Christ's ministry, not before creation, as seen in Luke 10:18 and Revelation 12.

scriptural_links.summary: God curses the serpent (devil) to eat dust and puts enmity between his seed and the woman's seed.
The fall of Helel (Lucifer) is a correction of the Babylonian succession myth, describing the devil's failed rebellion.
The Most High divided the nations according to the number of the sons of God (angels), referring to the Tower of Babel.
Jesus says, 'I saw Satan fall like lightning from heaven,' indicating a fall during his ministry.
The dragon (devil) and Satan are cast out, possibly as two figures or one figure falling twice.

glossary.definition: A pagan narrative where a younger god overthrows the most high god, corrected in Scripture to show the rebellion fails.
Giants born from the union of fallen angels (sons of God) and human women; their spirits become unclean demons.
A Babylonian term for territorial spirits, used in Deuteronomy 32:17 to describe demons that received worship.
A title meaning 'adversary,' possibly a distinct angelic figure who accuses in the divine council and falls during Christ's ministry.
Hebrew for 'shining one, son of the morning,' a name for the devil in Isaiah 14, possibly derived from Enlil.
